items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1979-12-05
items.q: One of them, I always met John Marrero

ctx.x: When you were coming up, you know like when you first started playing banjo, your idol was John Marrero. That's right.

One of them, I always met John Marrero, but John Sincero was living up in Chicago, I think, and I used to copy some of his stuff. And I actually copied some of Les Paul, the other guy who used to be with, Benny Goodman, a black fellow, he died. He's all a Christian. He's a great way. You have to do that to keep yourself voices down, you see.
What did you like about Marrero? I mean you took over, I mean you saw him quite a bit, I gather, down here. What about his playing did you like? I've never saw him.

items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1961-01-29
items.q: I remember him when he played with, uh, the Bay Rizley band... I know the whole family, but I don't remember who taught him.

ctx.x: Uh, go back to the, uh, going back to the early days a bit, uh, what can you remember about John Marrero, you know? What kind of stuff you remember?

Well, John Marrero was a fine banjo player. I remember him when he played with, uh, the Bay Rizley band, which Celestine was the trumpet player. Mm-hmm. Emma Barrett was the piano player. Uh, uh, Simon was the bass player. And, uh, uh, Paul Barberin was the clarinet and saxophone player. And, uh, I mean, yeah, Chani Fawcett, Abbie Fawcett was on drums, yeah. Oh, yeah. I remember he was a very fine banjo player. Mm-hmm.
Did, uh, were they, you know, you heard the records that he made, uh, John Marrero. Are they good examples of his playing, or did he play four or four most of the time?
